expert.item: amortized O(1) append already holds for any fixed growth factor g > 1 (Chapter 1's result); this topic doesn't reprove it

the memory-reuse argument: g = 2 means every new chunk is larger than the sum of every chunk freed before it, so the allocator can never satisfy a resize from the vector's own discards; any g < 2 eventually can

real libraries disagree on g: gcc's libstdc++ uses 2 (per Folly's own account), Folly's fbvector deliberately picks 1.5, CPython's list uses a much gentler ~1.125x + 6 policy, Rust's Vec explicitly declines to guarantee any factor at all
expert.source: Folly FBVector.md; CPython listobject.c; doc.rust-lang.org Vec docs

expert.item: reserve(n): a non-binding-in-effect-but-precisely-specified directive; reallocates iff current capacity < n; no reallocation on later insertions until size would exceed the reserved capacity
shrink_to_fit(): a non-binding request (the standard explicitly allows the implementation to ignore it); never increases capacity; may reallocate
reallocation invalidates every pointer, reference and iterator into the old buffer, including the past-the-end iterator; if no reallocation happens, they all remain valid
contiguous storage touches one cache line per B elements on a scan; a pointer-chased structure can touch one cache line per element if nodes aren't allocated in order
expert.source: Chapter 1 topic 2/10 (cache-lines, cache-miss); previewed here, measured in topic 2

expert.item: the growth-factor choice is a real, shipped engineering decision with measurable consequences (total bytes ever allocated, number of reallocations for a given final size), not a textbook abstraction
expert.source: examples.py: simulate g=2, g=1.5 and CPython's formula over the chapter's 1,000,000-append run
